mcqs.question: Why do high-throughput distributed systems typically prefer Snowflake-style IDs over plain UUIDs for primary keys?
options: UUIDs cannot guarantee uniqueness across machines
UUIDs are smaller in size and waste less storage
Snowflake IDs are mostly increasing, giving better index locality and rough time-sortability that random UUIDs lack
UUIDs require a central coordination service to generate
mcqs.explanation: Snowflake IDs are roughly increasing, which keeps B-tree inserts append-like and preserves time order — UUIDs are random, fragmenting indexes and carrying no time information. UUIDs are actually larger (128 bits) and are already fully decentralized; uniqueness isn't the issue, index behavior and sortability are.

mcqs.question: In a Snowflake-style system, what should stay fully decentralized even when machine-ID assignment uses a centralized coordination service?
options: The clock each machine reads from
The actual ID generation on every request
The bit layout of the 64-bit ID
The database that eventually stores the generated IDs
mcqs.explanation: Machine-ID assignment happens rarely (at startup) and can tolerate a brief coordination dependency; ID generation itself happens on nearly every write and must stay local with zero per-call coordination, or the whole design loses its scaling advantage. The clock, bit layout, and storage are unrelated to this specific trade-off.

mcqs.question: A machine's clock jumps backward by 50ms due to an NTP correction. What should its ID generator do?
options: Continue generating IDs using the new, lower clock reading
Reuse the last timestamp it already generated an ID with
Refuse to generate new IDs (or block) until the clock passes the last timestamp used
Switch permanently to a different machine ID
mcqs.explanation: Refusing or blocking briefly avoids ever emitting an ID that sorts before one already issued, and avoids the duplicate-ID risk of reusing a timestamp. Continuing with the lower clock value directly breaks ordering; a new machine ID doesn't address the clock problem at all.

mcqs.question: Two instances in an autoscaling group both end up with machine ID 42 due to a config drift. What's the actual consequence?
options: Both instances silently generate IDs that can collide, since uniqueness depends entirely on the machine-ID field being unique
The instances will automatically detect the conflict and one will shut down
Only the timestamp field is affected, sequence and machine ID remain safe
IDs will simply be generated more slowly on both machines
mcqs.explanation: Nothing in the ID format itself detects a duplicate machine ID — both machines will happily generate structurally valid IDs that can collide whenever their timestamp and sequence also line up. There's no automatic self-detection or shutdown, and this doesn't affect generation speed, only correctness.

mcqs.question: Why is freezing the timestamp field during a clock rollback more dangerous than briefly pausing ID generation?
options: Pausing generation is illegal under most SLAs
Freezing the timestamp has no real downside compared to pausing
It can produce a genuine duplicate ID if the sequence counter also wraps during the frozen window
Freezing the timestamp uses more CPU than pausing
mcqs.explanation: With a frozen timestamp, uniqueness rests entirely on the sequence field — if it also wraps during that window, two IDs can end up with identical timestamp and sequence bits, a true duplicate. A brief pause is recoverable and cheap; there's no SLA or CPU-cost angle that changes this trade-off.
